name: Vamanamoorthy Temple, Thrikkakara
deity: Vishnu as Vamana, the dwarf avatara — the Appan of Thirukkatkarai in the hymns — with the Goddess Perunchelvanayaki in Sri Vaishnava tradition
period: A Divya Desam of Malai Nadu, sung by Nammalvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham and remembered as the home of Onam
summary: At Thrikkakara in Kochi, Vishnu is worshipped as Vamana, the dwarf who humbled King Mahabali — a Malai Nadu Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar, and the temple most closely bound to Kerala's festival of Onam.

sections.history: Thrikkakara, now within the city of Kochi, is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and is counted among the shrines of Malai Nadu; Nammalvar sang its lord as the Appan of Thirukkatkarai. It is one of the few temples in India whose presiding deity is Vamana, the dwarf avatara. Around eighteen stone inscriptions from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries, the age of the Chera Perumals, have been found here, and they tell of chieftains gathering at Thrikkakara to honour the king during Onam — then a festival of many days. The shrine itself may well be older than its earliest records.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Kerala manner: a sanctum (srikovil) beneath sloping roofs, enclosed by the nalambalam cloister, with a tall flagstaff on the approach and a broad compound where the Onam crowds gather. Close by stands a shrine of Shiva. The old stone inscriptions, cut in the Vattezhuthu script of medieval Kerala, are a quiet treasure of the precinct and one of the region's important records of the Chera age.
sections.legends: The puranas tell how the generous asura king Mahabali, ruler of the three worlds, was approached by Vamana, a dwarf brahmin boy, who asked for three paces of land. When the gift was granted, Vamana grew to cosmic size, measuring earth and sky in two strides, and for the third Mahabali offered his own head. Kerala tradition places Mahabali's realm at Thrikkakara and holds that the beloved king was granted leave to visit his people once a year — the homecoming that Onam celebrates. Tradition reads the name itself as 'the place of the sacred foot'.
sections.festivals: Onam is the temple's great festival: a ten-day utsavam in the Malayalam month of Chingam (August–September) that begins on Atham and culminates on Thiruvonam, with the flag hoisted, the lord taken in procession and the whole town in celebration. Households across Kerala lay their Onam floral carpets in the same ten-day rhythm. Vaikunta Ekadashi is also observed.
sections.experience: Visit during Onam to see Thrikkakara at its most joyful, when the temple becomes the heart of Kerala's harvest festival — or come on an ordinary morning for quiet darshan. In this place the story honours both the god and the king he humbled: Onam is a festival of Mahabali's homecoming as much as of Vamana's grace. Pause by the Shiva shrine and the old inscribed stones.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan and a midday closure, following the temple's own schedule; festival days are crowded. Confirm current timings locally before you visit.
visit.dressCode: Traditional dress is expected: by Kerala temple custom men usually enter bare-chested in a mundu or dhoti, and women in saree or other traditional dress; footwear is left outside. Follow posted rules and the guidance of temple staff.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in and around the sanctum; follow posted rules and the guidance of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Thrikkakara is in Kochi, Ernakulam district, close to Edappally and Kakkanad, and is easily reached by road and city bus. Ernakulam Junction is the main railway station, and Cochin International Airport at Nedumbassery is about 20 km away.
